What is the Bhagavad Gita about?

The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna, spoken on the battlefield of Kurukshetra just before war begins. Arjuna loses his will to fight, and Krishna teaches him about duty (dharma), selfless action (karma yoga), knowledge (jnana yoga), devotion (bhakti yoga), the immortal self, and how to live without being ruled by results. The closing teaching is to take refuge in the divine and act with courage (Bhagavad Gita 1.1-2, 18.63, 18.66).

Why was Arjuna unwilling to fight in the war?

Arjuna sees his own kinsmen, teachers, elders and friends standing on the battlefield and is overcome. His limbs fail him, his mouth dries up, his hair stands on end and his bow slips from his hand (Bhagavad Gita 1.28-30). He grieves that the destruction of family dharma will corrupt society (1.40-44). Rather than acting from that despair, he surrenders the question to Krishna: he becomes Krishna's student and asks to be instructed (2.7).

What can we learn from Arjuna's despair?

Arjuna was a great warrior, yet he was paralysed by doubt at the moment of decision. The Gita's first answer is gentle: grief for those who should not be grieved and sorrow where there is no room for sorrow are not the mark of the wise (Bhagavad Gita 2.11). The lesson is that even the capable need a teacher and first principles. Arjuna recovers by becoming a student again (2.7), not by suppressing his feelings.

What does the Gita say about the decline of a family or community?

Krishna explains that when duty in a family decays, disorder spreads through the family, the streets and the villages (Bhagavad Gita 1.40-43). He calls the loss of inherited duty the worst of sins, because it destroys the ancestral way of life (1.44). The point is social: when small duties collapse, mixing of classes follows, and no one can be happy (1.41-42).

Who actually spoke and narrated the Bhagavad Gita?

The teaching itself was spoken by Krishna to Arjuna on the battlefield. It reaches King Dhritarashtra through Sanjaya, his charioteer, who was granted divine sight to see and hear the war (Bhagavad Gita 1.1-2). Sanjaya closes the account by reporting Arjuna's words after the teaching: his delusion is destroyed and he is ready to act (18.73). The dialogue sits inside the Mahabharata and is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa.

Is the Bhagavad Gita only a war story?

The battlefield is the setting, not the subject. The war is the pressure that forces the real question: how should a person act when duty and desire conflict? Krishna's answers are about the inner war - desire, anger, fear and ego - and apply to any life: work without clinging to results (Bhagavad Gita 2.47), see the self in all beings (5.18), and take refuge in the divine (18.66). The outer war only frames that teaching.

What does the Bhagavad Gita say about death?

The Gita teaches that the self is never born and never dies (Bhagavad Gita 2.20). Just as a person puts off old clothes and puts on new ones, the self casts off one body and enters another (2.22). Death is certain for the born and birth is certain for the dead, so there is no cause to grieve for anyone (2.27). Krishna uses this to steady Arjuna: what changes is the body, not you.

Is the soul born or unborn according to the Gita?

The self is unborn, eternal, permanent and ancient - it is not slain when the body is slain (Bhagavad Gita 2.20). Where the self is, there can be no coming into being; where there is coming into being, there can be no ceasing to be (2.16). The self only appears to change because it passes from childhood to youth to old age, and then into another body (2.13).

What is karma yoga in simple terms?

Karma yoga is acting without attachment to the fruits of the action. You have a right to your work, never to its results (Bhagavad Gita 2.47). Establish yourself in yoga - inner steadiness - and perform action, treating success and failure alike (2.48). One who offers all action into awareness, acting without clinging, becomes free of guilt (5.10). In short: do your job fully, do not clutch at the outcome.

Explain Bhagavad Gita chapter 2 verse 47 in simple words.

Bhagavad Gita 2.47 says: you have a claim to action alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruits of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. Practically, it means give your full effort to the work in front of you, and stop treating the reward - praise, money, promotion, even success - as the price of your effort. The result depends on many things beyond you; the effort is entirely yours.

Should I stop caring about results entirely?

Not caring and not clinging are different. The Gita asks you to drop attachment to results, not interest in them: plan well, work well, review outcomes - but do not stake your peace on them (Bhagavad Gita 2.47-48). Acting with skill and without craving for reward is what purifies action (2.50). Krishna never tells Arjuna to be careless; he tells him to be steady whether the result is won or lost.

How can I stay balanced during success and failure?

Krishna tells Arjuna to be established in yoga and perform action, remaining even-minded in success and failure (Bhagavad Gita 2.48). That balance, called equanimity, is the foundation of freedom from sin (2.48) and of skill in action (2.50). The person of steady wisdom is neither shaken by sorrow nor carried away by pleasure (2.56). Balance is trained by noticing both outcomes as passing weather, not as verdicts about you.

Who is the person of steady wisdom described in chapter 2?

The sthitaprajna, the person of steady wisdom, is described at Bhagavad Gita 2.55-57: when desire has been renounced, such a person rests in the self alone, is not shaken by sorrow or elated by pleasure, withdraws the senses from their objects like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, and gives up attachment even for taste. By contemplation such a mind becomes steady, and at the end such a person attains peace (2.65, 2.71-72).
